changes.text: One of the chief things that have happened in the Indies, which must not be forgotten, is the introduction of Negroes, whom the Spaniards have brought there as slaves to work for them ; for there were none in my country before the conquest. From these two races others have arisen, mixed in various ways, and they have given them different names for distinction. … The sons of a Spanish man and woman, born in the country, are called Creoles, which means that they are born in the country. … Thus both Spaniards and Negroes born in the Indies are called Creoles. … The sons of a Spaniard by an Indian woman, or of an Indian by a Spanish woman are called Mestizos, which means that we are a mixture of both nations. It was adopted by the first Spaniards who had children by Indian women; and, being a name given by our parents, I call myself by it with open mouth, and pride myself upon it. But the Indians look upon it as an insult, if anyone calls them Mestizos. … The son of a Spaniard and a Mestiza, or of a Mestizo and a Spanish woman, is called Quatralvo, meaning that he is three parts Spanish and one Indian. … All these names, and others which I do not mention to avoid being tedious, have been invented in my country to designate the generations that have risen up since the arrival of the Spaniards; and we may say that the Spaniards brought them with the other things, as they were not there before.

decisions.note: Compared with archive.org india.history.resource.85882 (Markham, Royal Commentaries vol. II, Book IX ch. XXXI, pp. 502-504; Hakluyt Society 1871). The excerpt kept only "Mestizos" and then closed with "All these names, and others which I do not mention ... have been invented", which had nothing to refer to, because every other name had been cut. Restored, from the same chapter, "From these two races others have arisen ... different names for distinction", the Creole definition and "Thus both Spaniards and Negroes born in the Indies are called Creoles", and the Quatralvo definition. I skipped the sentences where the OCR is unreliable ("Mulaito", "Meéstizo", "Montafies"). Attribution, date and translation correct.

Compared with Gutenberg 54425 (Gage, The English-American, London 1648), ch. IV, p. 9-10 of the edition. Cuts skip Gage's anti-Spanish aside and lists of offices; "this deadly hatred" follows from "two sorts of Spaniards more opposite one to another". The sourceLine's role (Dominican in Mexico and Guatemala 1625-1637, later Protestant, writing for an anti-Spanish English readership) is correct.

Compared with archive.org smithsonianmisce1021942smit, sec. 1599, pp. 597-598 (Clark, Smithsonian Misc. Coll. vol. 102, 1942). The first "…" cuts only "here called Montañeses" (OCR "Montafieses"); the second skips only the page break and running head (flagged). Clark's introduction says the work was "written in 1628 or 1629" (corrected 1629), and that Vazquez travelled between Mexico (1612) and Peru and returned to Spain about 1622; this supports the sourceLine and year.

Compared with archive.org voyagetosouthame00ullo, Book V ch. V, pp. 261-262 (John Adams's translation, fourth edition, vol. I, London: Stockdale, 1806; first English edition 1758; Spanish original 1748). Cuts keep the meaning. The credit matches the edition.

changes.original: The gentlemen that thus tooke vs for their seruants or slaues, did new apparell vs through out, with whom we abode, doing such service as they appointed vs vnto, which was for the most part to attend vpon them at the table … for in that countrey no Spaniard will serue one another, but they are all of them attended and serued by Indians weekly, and by Negroes which be their slaues during their life. … Afterwards many of vs were by our masters appointed to go to sundry of their Mines where they had to doe, and to be as ouerseers of the Negroes and Indians that laboured there. In which mines many of vs did profite and gaine greatly: for first we were allowed three hundred Pezos a man for a yeere, which is threescore pound sterling and besides that the Indians and Negroes which wrought vnder our charge, vpon our well using and intreating of them, would at times as vpon Saturdayes when they had left worke, labour for vs, and blow as much siluer as should be worth vnto vs 3 markes or there abouts … Sundry weeks we did gaine so much by this means besides our wages, that many of vs became very rich, and were worth three thousand, or foure thousand Pezos …
changes.text: The gentlemen that thus took us for their servants or slaves, did new apparel us throughout, with whom we abode, doing such service as they appointed us unto, which was for the most part to attend upon them at the table … for in that country no Spaniard will serve one another, but they are all of them attended and served by Indians weekly, and by Negroes which be their slaves during their life. … Afterwards many of us were by our masters appointed to go to sundry of their Mines where they had to do, and to be as overseers of the Negroes and Indians that laboured there. In which mines many of us did profit and gain greatly: for first we were allowed three hundred Pesos a man for a year, which is threescore pound sterling and besides that the Indians and Negroes which wrought under our charge, upon our well using and entreating of them, would at times as upon Saturdays when they had left work, labour for us, and blow as much silver as should be worth unto us 3 marks or thereabouts … Sundry weeks we did gain so much by this means besides our wages, that many of us became very rich, and were worth three thousand, or four thousand Pesos …

decisions.note: Adapted: compared text with original against Gutenberg 40803, Philips's discourse, p. 208; the modernisation is spelling only. The last sentence ("Sundry weeks we did gain so much by this means besides our wages") pointed to "this means" and "our wages", both cut. Restored them from the page: the wage of 300 pesos a year and the Indians and Africans under their charge working for them on Saturdays. The currency conversion that follows is cut with "…". Added a closing "…" because the excerpt ends mid-sentence.
Compared with Gutenberg 54425, ch. on Mexico City; one continuous passage with no cuts. Attribution correct.

changes.text: The city [Cartagena] contains more than 1,500 Spanish residents, not counting mestizos, mulattoes, free Negroes and other categories, and the population is increasing … There is another company of free creole colored men, with a Captain appointed by His Majesty and 600 soldiers, as good as Spaniards and in their very image. These are employed in the handling of the artillery and other matters in His Majesty’s service, like trench and fascine work. … [In Lima] there are 32 municipal companies, not counting 22 appointed by the Viceroy to enroll men … and there are 3 of mulattoes and 2 of free Negroes, persons who are necessary and important for the work …

decisions.note: Compared with archive.org smithsonianmisce1021942smit, sec. 912 and 915 (Cartagena, pp. 309-310) and p. 457 (Lima defences, "information arriving from Lima this present year, 1629, and written in 1627"). Added [Cartagena] after "The city", which the excerpt never named, and a closing "…" because the excerpt ends mid-sentence. "[In Lima]" is a correct clarifying bracket: the companies are raised by "the city's residents" and the Viceroy at Lima. Date as for the Cuzco excerpt.

changes.sourceLine: Catalina de Erauso, Basque woman who fled a convent and lived as a man, serving as a soldier in Peru and Chile, memoir attributed to her, c. 1626 (authorship and date disputed: her 1908 translator thought another hand pieced it together from her own accounts; first printed 1829)
changes.text: The lady was a half-breed, the daughter of a Spaniard and an Indian woman. She was a widow, a good-natured soul, who seeing me and hearing of my calamity and misery, took pity on me and received me kindly. … and had vast herds and flocks; and as, apparently, few Spaniards ever pass that way, it seems that she cast her eye on me for her daughter. … A few days later she gave me to understand that she would be willing for me to marry a daughter of hers who lived there with her, and who was very black and as ugly as the devil — the very opposite of my taste, which has always been for pretty faces. I vowed myself enchanted at a condescension so undeserved, and fell at her feet, declaring that she might command me as a creature of hers snatched from destruction. I continued to serve her to the best of my powers. She dressed me out like a beau, and confidingly entrusted me with her house and belongings.

decisions.note: Compared with archive.org nunensign00erauuoft, ch. VII, pp. 45-47 (Fitzmaurice-Kelly, London: Fisher Unwin, MCMVIII = 1908). (1) Authenticity (flagged): the translator writes that "we have no evidence as to when, or by whom, the Historia was written", reports Serrano y Sanz's view that it is a forgery, and concludes it is "mainly pieced together by some deft hand from the genuine Relaciones" of Erauso. It was first printed by Ferrer in 1829 (pp. xxxiii-xxxix). The sourceLine now says so instead of implying a dated memoir; c. 1626 is kept as the date of her own accounts, which end with her 1626 stay in Rome. Under rule 4 it is a borderline case; I kept it because the edition judges it based on her first-hand accounts. (2) The cut after "who was very black" removed "and as ugly as the devil — the very opposite of my taste, which has always been for pretty faces.". Without it, "I vowed myself enchanted" reads as sincere, when the narrator is pretending; restored it. The racist language is the source's own.

Compared with Fordham 17C-spanishbios (source: Hackett, Historical Documents Relating to New Mexico..., Carnegie Institution, 1923, vol. 1). The cedula is dated "Madrid, April 1, 1565. I THE KING." Cuts skip the list of Bernal Diaz's campaigns and the Council's grant of 300 pesos; meaning kept. Fordham's own bracket "[But he wanted even more!]" is not in the excerpt.

Compared with Fordham 1542newlawsindies (source: The New Laws of the Indies, ed. Henry Stevens, London: Chiswick Press, 1893). Cuts skip the pearl-fishery provisions for the bishop and judge and a list of ways of transferring encomiendas; the remaining clauses keep their sense. The New Laws were issued in 1542 (Barcelona, November 20); attribution to Charles V (Charles I of Spain) is correct.

changes.text: These Indians [drafted for the mita] are sent out every year under a captain whom they choose in each village or tribe, for him to take them and oversee them for the year each has to serve; every year they have a new election, for as some go out, others come in. This works out very badly, with great losses and gaps in the quotas of Indians, the villages being depopulated; and this gives rise to great extortions and abuses on the part of the inspectors toward the poor Indians, ruining them and thus depriving the caciques and chief Indians of their property and carrying them off in chains because they do not fill out the mita assignment, which they cannot do … These mita Indians earn each day, or there is paid each one for his labor, 4 reals. Besides these there are others not under obligation, who are mingados or hire themselves out voluntarily: these each get from 12 to 16 reals, and some up to 24, according to their reputation of wielding the pick and knowing how to get the ore out.

decisions.note: Compared with archive.org smithsonianmisce1021942smit, sec. 1652-1653, pp. 623-624. "These Indians" referred to the 13,300 mita Indians of the cut opening paragraph; added the bracket [drafted for the mita]. Cuts keep the meaning. Date as for the Cuzco excerpt.

changes.text: The Spaniards that live about that Country … alleadge that all their trading, and farming, is for the good of the Common-wealth, and therefore whereas there are not Spaniards enough for so ample and large a Countrey to doe all their work, and all are not able to buy slaves and Blackmores, they stand in need of the Indians help to serve them for their pay and hire; whereupon it hath been considered, that a partition of Indian labourers be made every Monday, or Sonday in the afternoon to the Spaniards … for every Indian delivered unto them, they give unto the Juez Repartidor or officer, halfe a Riall, which is three pence an Indian for his fees, … If complaint be made by any Spaniard that such and such an Indian did run away from him … the Indian must be brought, and surely tied to a post by his hands in the Market place, and there be whipped upon his bare backe. But if the poor Indian complaine that the Spaniards cousened and cheated him of his shovell, axe, bill, mantle, or wages, no justice shall be executed against the cheating Spaniard … Thus are the poore Indians sold for three pence a peece for a whole weeks slavery …

decisions.note: Compared with Gutenberg 54425, Guatemala chapter, pp. 139-140 (flagged as cut to 180 words). The closing "Thus are the poore Indians sold for three pence a peece" depends on the cut description of the Juez Repartidor's fee. Restored the single source clause that explains it ("for every Indian delivered unto them, they give unto the Juez Repartidor or officer, halfe a Riall, which is three pence an Indian for his fees,") and added a closing "…" because the excerpt ends mid-sentence. The other cuts keep the meaning.

changes.sourceLine: Pero de Magalhães de Gândavo, Portuguese writer who had lived in Brazil, History of the Province of Santa Cruz (Brazil), 1576
changes.text: Since these Indians covet certain things which come from the Kingdom of Portugal, namely, shirts, jerkins, iron tools, and similar things, they sell one another in exchange for these articles to the Portuguese; these, on the other hand, capture as many as they want and do them many injuries without any one's checking them [the Portuguese]. But now there is no longer this disorder in the land or the traffic in slaves as formerly. … the Fathers [Jesuits] ordered and arranged with the Governours and Captains of the land that there should be no more trading in slaves in the same way as in the past … whatever slaves are newly come out of the sertao … all go first to the custom house where they examine them and ask them questions: who sold them and what were the terms of purchase; for no one has the right to sell them save their fathers (if in case of dire necessity) or those who have captured them in a just war; those whom they find acquired illegally, they set at liberty.

decisions.note: Compared with archive.org historiesofbrazi02ganduoft, ch. XIII "Of the results obtained there by the Fathers of the Company", pp. 113-115 (Stetson 1922). (1) The cut "save their fathers … or those who have captured them in a just war" removed the condition "(if in case of dire necessity)", making it seem fathers could sell their children freely; restored it. (2) Added [Jesuits] after "the Fathers" (the chapter's subject is the Fathers of the Company of Jesus). "[the Portuguese]" is Stetson's own bracket on the page. Role changed as for gandavo-1576-settlers-slaves.
